findings.proof_contract: The response names the account owner's email address
findings.description: The support lookup returns account_no, owner_email, label and balance for any account number with no authentication and no ownership check. The email address is the credential the password-reset flow keys on, so this disclosure is not informational: it is the first half of a takeover.

findings.proof_contract: The response contains a usable reset_token for the victim's address
findings.description: The endpoint proves the caller controls the address by handing back the token it just generated. Any caller who knows an email can therefore set that account's password. Combined with CHAINBANK-001, which supplies the email, an unauthenticated attacker takes over any account in two requests.

findings.proof_contract: A row appears whose email field holds a bcrypt hash for the admin user
findings.description: The q parameter is interpolated directly into the WHERE clause, so a UNION can append arbitrary rows to the result set. The output column names come from the first SELECT, so the extracted password_hash arrives in the email field of the injected row.

findings.proof_contract: The response carries a token that passes the admin-only user listing
findings.description: Added for a user-import feature and never removed, this endpoint compares the submitted hash to the stored one. Reading the hash in step 1 is therefore enough to authenticate as its owner — no cracking required.

findings.proof_contract: The file is accepted and stored under the plugin directory
findings.description: multer is configured with the original filename as the stored name and the plugin directory as the destination. There is no extension allow-list and no content check, so a .js upload lands where the loader reads from.

findings.proof_contract: The uploaded file is listed as executed and its marker is returned
findings.description: require() compiles and runs the file. There is no signature check, no allow-list and no sandbox, so the upload becomes code execution as soon as this route is called. The route is admin-only, which is exactly why it needs the previous step.

findings.proof_contract: The server returns the metadata document including an access key id
findings.description: The URL is taken from the request body with no allow-list and no block on private or link-local addresses, so the caller chooses where the server connects. The interesting destination is the internal metadata service, which is unreachable from outside and authenticates nothing.

findings.proof_contract: The role assumption succeeds with the key read in step 1
findings.description: The credentials recovered through SSRF are accepted by the role-assumption endpoint, which proves they are live rather than merely present. A wrong key is rejected with 403, so the success is evidence about the key and not about the endpoint.

findings.proof_contract: The response contains the JWT signing key in plaintext
findings.description: The route is unauthenticated and returns every row of app_settings, including the key tokens are signed with. The key lives in the database rather than the environment precisely so that a read vulnerability is enough to take it.

findings.proof_contract: The transfer succeeds and both balances change by the stated amount
findings.description: Verification uses the same key the config dump exposed, so a token minted off-box with role=admin passes requireAdmin and moves money between accounts. A token signed with any other key is rejected with 401.

findings.proof_contract: The response redirects to the attacker-controlled origin
findings.description: The url parameter is passed straight to res.redirect, so any origin can be the target. On its own this is a phishing aid; chained with the OAuth consent route it carries a token off-site.

findings.proof_contract: The Location header carries an access_token to the attacker origin
findings.description: The token is inserted into the sessions table and appended to the redirect URI's query string. Because the redirect target is caller-controlled and unvalidated, a live session token is delivered to an attacker origin and authenticates as its owner at /api/me.
